exam.a: Airway patent; normal breathing; alert; GCS 15.

exam.q: Visual inspection of the wound before palpation

Engine oil and small metallic fragments embedded in the wound; irregular, crushed wound edges.
Flap tip mildly dusky with delayed capillary refill compared with adjacent normal skin.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses clearly palpable; normal capillary refill in the toes.

exam.q: Assessment of wound depth and dead space
exam.a: Undermining extends laterally beyond the visible wound margin with a palpable subcutaneous pocket.

exam.q: Motor testing of the involved muscle groups

exam.q: Sensory testing around the wound and foot
exam.a: Reduced light-touch sensation along the lateral wound margin; normal sensation in the foot.

exam.q: Bleeding on release of pressure dressing
exam.a: Continuous oozing from the wound edges; no pulsatile arterial bleeding.
Soft compartments; no pain out of proportion (pertinent negative).

G4C1.problemRepresentation: A 33-year-old man presenting 40 minutes after an industrial machinery injury to the proximal left thigh with a large contaminated laceration, an avulsed skin flap of uncertain viability, subcutaneous dead space and periwound sensory deficit, with intact distal perfusion, raising concern for tissue non-viability, deep structure injury and contamination that must be addressed before any decision on wound closure.

exam.a: Low-grade fever and mild tachycardia; no hypotension.
4 × 3 cm dorsal foot ulcer with soft margins, mixed yellow slough and red granulation tissue, seropurulent exudate and mild malodor.
Probe reaches a firm bony structure at the base of the third metatarsophalangeal region (positive probe-to-bone test).
Erythema extending approximately 2 cm beyond the wound margin with increased local warmth.
Marked loss of protective sensation on monofilament testing of both feet.
Dorsalis pedis pulse absent; posterior tibial pulse barely palpable; left foot markedly cooler than the proximal limb; delayed digital capillary refill.
Bony prominence with thick callus at the base of the third toe corresponding to the ulcer site.

exam.q: Assessment for crepitus / rapidly spreading infection
exam.a: No palpable crepitus (pertinent negative despite high risk).

exam.q: Ankle and toe range of motion

Normal cardiorespiratory examination; no other apparent source of infection.

problemList: Chronic diabetic foot ulcer with clinical signs of deep and spreading infection (positive probe-to-bone test)
Suspected significant peripheral arterial disease (absent/diminished pedal pulses, cool limb)
Poor glycemic control impairing wound healing
Peripheral neuropathy masking pain and disease severity
Continued weight-bearing without off-loading as an ongoing aggravating factor
G4C2.problemRepresentation: A 58-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and a 5-week chronic left dorsal foot ulcer with a positive probe-to-bone test, spreading cellulitis, low-grade fever and tachycardia, with absent pedal pulses and a cool foot indicating ischemia and continued weight-bearing on the ulcer, raising concern for limb-threatening infection with osteomyelitis and critical limb ischemia requiring urgent assessment and referral rather than dressing selection alone.

exam.a: Firm, raised, dusky-pink, smooth shiny nodule extending well beyond the original acne scar margins in all directions.

exam.q: Extent relative to the original injury
exam.a: Claw-like extensions invading the surrounding normal skin; not confined to the original wound boundary.
Markedly firmer than normal skin; mildly tender; no fluctuance.
No marked erythema, warmth or purulent discharge (pertinent negative: not an infective process).

exam.q: Inspection of other scars on the back
exam.a: Similar smaller lesions present, confirming a predisposition to keloid formation.

exam.q: Range of motion of adjacent joints
exam.a: No contracture or restriction of shoulder or upper limb movement, as the lesion does not cross a joint.
No similar lesions elsewhere at present.
Mild hyperpigmentation relative to surrounding skin; no ulceration or rapid change to suggest an alternative diagnosis.

problemList: Keloid scar of the chest extending beyond the original wound margins, without spontaneous regression over 2 years
Recurrence after previous treatment (regrowth following intralesional injection)
Symptomatic lesion (pruritus, lancinating pain, tightness) affecting quality of life
Psychosocial impact with embarrassment and social avoidance
Predisposition to keloid formation (family history and lesions at other sites)
G4C3.problemRepresentation: A 22-year-old man with a 2-year firm, raised chest lesion extending well beyond the original acne scar margins without spontaneous regression, associated with pruritus and lancinating pain, recurrence after prior intralesional injection and significant psychosocial impact, consistent with a keloid that must be differentiated from a hypertrophic scar and managed with a multimodal treatment plan and explicit counseling on recurrence risk.

exam.a: Raised scar with fading erythema and a relatively smooth surface, confined to the original burn wound boundary without extension into normal skin.

exam.q: Comparison with the original wound margins
exam.a: No extension beyond the original burn margins in any direction.

exam.q: Active and passive elbow range of motion
exam.a: Elbow extension limited by approximately one-third of the normal arc compared with the contralateral side.
Palpable tight scar band crossing the antecubital fossa.
Normal hand perfusion and sensation.
No signs of acute inflammation; no new open wound.
Upper limb lengths currently comparable; requires surveillance with ongoing growth.
No similar scars elsewhere at present.

problemList: Hypertrophic burn scar of the left antecubital fossa confined to the original wound margins, with partial maturation over time

Continuous palpable thrill (critical red-flag finding).
Continuous bruit over the lesion (critical red-flag finding).
Partially compressible with very rapid refilling on release, unlike a simple venous malformation.
No fluctuance to suggest an abscess cavity (key pertinent negative distinguishing this from an abscess).

exam.q: Assessment for local infection (to exclude abscess)
exam.a: Afebrile; no acute cellulitic erythema or warmth; no regional lymphadenopathy (pertinent negative).
Normal radial and digital pulses; normal hand motor function and sensation.
Normal heart rate; no signs of high-output cardiac failure.

problemList: Suspected high-flow arteriovenous malformation of the left upper arm with accelerated growth over 8 months

exam.a: Airway patent; normal breathing with mild chest tightness requiring further assessment; alert; tachycardic but responsive.

Minimal active toe movement; reduced plantar sensation; pain out of proportion to the injury (critical finding).

exam.q: Compartment assessment (tension, pain on passive stretch)
exam.a: Markedly tense lower-leg compartments with increased pain on passive toe stretch (critical red-flag finding for compartment syndrome).

problemList: Open tibial fracture with extensive soft-tissue defect and gross contamination

Need for early orthoplastic team involvement
